lesson.menu_desc: Reading about why series are so hard to stop -- cliffhangers, autoplay, plot twists -- and talking about your own viewing habits: I avoid watching, I decided to stop -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- Just One More Episode
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mirela Lapera | Lesson 2 -- Just One More Episode
lesson.grammar_point: gerund x infinitive after verbs: enjoy / avoid / finish / keep + -ing; want / decide / need / plan + to; -ing after a preposition (tired of watching); stop watching x stop to watch

listenings.text: Here's what happens. When an episode ends with a cliffhanger, your brain feels that the story isn't finished. And the brain hates unfinished stories. It wants to know what happens next, so you keep watching. Then autoplay makes it even easier. You don't need to decide to continue. You only need to do nothing. And doing nothing is the easiest thing in the world at eleven o'clock at night. So my advice is simple. Turn off autoplay, and decide how many episodes you will watch before you start, not after. It sounds small, but it really works.

My friends think I'm crazy. I've watched the same sitcom about six times. I know every joke. But that's exactly why I love it. After a hard day at work, I don't want to think. I don't want a plot twist or a cliffhanger. I just want to laugh with characters I know. It helps me relax. New series are different. They're great, but they're too addictive. If I start one on a Tuesday, I stay up until two in the morning. So during the week, I avoid starting new series. I keep those for the weekend, and on weeknights, I rewatch my old friends.

When I was a student, I watched a lot of American series, always with subtitles in my own language. I enjoyed the stories, but my English didn't improve much. One day, a teacher told me to try English subtitles. At first it was hard. I understood very little, and I wanted to give up. But I decided to keep going, one episode a day. I chose a sitcom that I already knew, so the story was easy to follow. After a few months, something changed. I stopped needing the subtitles for most of the dialogue. Today I teach English, and I still tell my students the same thing: keep watching, but change the subtitles.

paras: It is eleven at night. You planned to go to bed after one episode, but the episode ends with a cliffhanger, and the next one starts in ten seconds. You decide to watch just one more. Two hours later, you are still on the sofa. If this sounds familiar, you are not alone: millions of people binge-watch every week, and most of them say they want to watch less.

This is not an accident. Streaming companies want you to keep watching, and they design their series for that. Writers put a plot twist or a cliffhanger at the end of almost every episode, so your brain needs to know what happens next. Autoplay does the rest: you don't need to choose to continue; you need to choose to stop. Psychologists say that this small difference is the reason why series are so addictive.

So what can you do? Some people avoid starting a new series during the week. Others decide to watch only one episode a night and turn off autoplay. And some people use the habit to learn something new. If you enjoy watching series, try watching them in the original language, with subtitles in the same language. You will still get hooked on the story, but this time your English will thank you.
